newsitem.title: HAITI: FEATURE-Impoverished Haiti hopes to cut food imports.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Impoverished Haiti hopes to cut food imports.

text.p: Jadette Feryie sighs as she looks at a deteriorating banana field. There has never been a worse time for farming in Haiti, she says -- and she should know.

Feryie, who is 110, has farmed her bananas through dictatorships, coups and two U.S. occupations, including the 1994 arrival of U.S. soldiers whose successors linger in Haiti today. Over the same 11 decades, she has seen the steady disappearance of the impoverished Caribbean nation's trees in a spiral of deforestation that has robbed it of nutrient-rich topsoil and made the always hardscrabble existence of Haiti's many farmers even more desperate.

"This is the first year we haven't even been able to send our children to school," Feryie said as she sat with her family amid the scent of cooking fish and boiling bananas in the Arcahaie Plain, an hour's drive north of Port-au-Prince.

About 70 percent of Haiti's population lives off the land, most using simple tools and bare hands to scratch out a meagre existence. But with the loss of topsoil necessary for productive farming, thousands of peasants have been fleeing for Haiti's sprawling urban slums.

With government in upheaval -- the 1994 U.S. occupation ended a three-year military dictatorship and a U.S.-led trade embargo -- little attention had been given to agriculture until recently and even less to the loss of Haiti's trees.

Since his inauguration early this year, President Rene Preval has pledged to increase food production. Haiti's farmers satisfy barely half of the nation's food needs, according to the Agency for International Development.

On Oct. 17, Preval took most of his cabinet to the Artibonite rice-growing region, the most important of Haiti's agricultural zones, where he toured fields, opened an office and touted his plans to boost food production. "We have got to follow through on this," he said.
Haiti's parliament recently approved a plan to privatise nine state industries, which officials said could generate millions of dollars for the agriculture plan.

"Until the late 70's, Haiti's agricultural production was sufficient for our population," Agriculture Ministry Adviser Franck Hyppolite told Reuters. "Our country doesn't have a lot of mineral resources and we are undeveloped. Agriculture is the economic base of our country."

The agriculture programme in the Artibonite was funded by an $8 million Inter-American Development Bank loan. Agronomists said the region in the north is capable of producing rice for most of Haiti. Most Haitians prefer smaller-grain Artibonite rice to imported rice, but foreign marketers who can produce more rice for lower prices have flooded Haiti's markets.

"It is hard to have a social consciousness to buy Haitian rice when you need to buy rice to feed an entire family. Rice that comes from Miami is cheaper," Olkine Luis, a banana planter and mother of five, said.
Rice and banana growers have demanded an import tax, claiming foreign products are destroying the local market. But the government sees it differently.

"Since the 60's the tactic has been to raise taxes on foreign products to encourage local production, but that never works. Our goal is to help the producers produce better," Commerce Minister Fresnel Germain said.

The Preval administration hopes irrigation, credit for farmers and a strict policy of agrarian reform will organise and empower local producers. But critics say this formula is missing a vital component -- solutions to the nation's pressing environmental problems.

Less than three percent of Haiti's tree cover remains, and without it 15,000 acres (6,000 hectares) of arable land are lost yearly, according to a USAID report. "Deforestation occured on a widespread level under dictator Francois Duvalier, who had many areas in the country deforested to prohibit dissenting factions from hiding in the mountains," ecologist Felix Joseph said.

Farmers said Preval's pledge to help them had given them some hope but was not enough to counter the grim realities of subsistence farming on the deforested hillsides and rocky fields of the hemisphere's poorest nation.
"To die in Haiti is to escape from misery," Feryie said, squinting in the hot sun in her small village.
